newsitem.title: GERMANY: PROSIEBEN IS FIRST GERMAN TV GROUP TO GO PUBLIC.
newsitem.headline: PROSIEBEN IS FIRST GERMAN TV GROUP TO GO PUBLIC.

text.p: German TV group ProSieben Media AG aims to raise up to 1.26 billion marks ($728.6 million) in one of Germany's most highly publicised share offerings since last year's Deutsche Telekom AG issue.
The company, the first German television group to go public, said on Monday the 17.5 million preference shares would be offered to investors in a range of 66-72 marks a share.
"With the exception of Telekom, no other listing of a German company has generated as much public interest as the ProSieben share," said Georg Kofler, the company's chairman.
The final price will be announced on July 5 during ProSieben's nightly news broadcast at 1730 GMT. Shares begin trading on July 7.
The IPO range, to be discussed with institutional investors during the subscription period that begins on June 24 and ends on July 3, was largely in line with expectations of 62-80 marks.
Based on the range, the offer would be worth between 1.155 and 1.260 billion marks. The company's market capitalisation would be between 2.3 billion marks and 2.5 billion.
Analysts have said that interest for European and particularly German media stocks was high because there were so few listed companies in the fast-changing sector.
Pierre Drach, head of Frankfurt-based equity analysis Independent Research, said, "I'm surprised at how cheap it is, we had expected 68 to 78."
"I now expect we will get a bookbuilding price of 72 marks which I would be very pleased with and we recommend subscribing to the shares."
"But I wouldn't necessarily recommend buying them at 100 marks, it could be that we would issue a sell recommendation if the shares hit that level," he said.

The shares surged in grey market dealings after the group released the bookbuilding price range. ProSieben shares were bid at 100 marks and offered at 110 marks, according to broker Schnigge+Partner GmbH of Duesseldorf. ProSieben said that the price range of its initial public offering of 66-72 marks still left room for share price gains when the stock begins trading.

Kofler, speaking at a news conference, dismissed criticism that the IPO range was too high. Based on the company's price earnings ratio, forecast to be around 18 next year, the price was lower than the market average.
"If we remain below the market average, then it will be shown that we were relatively humble and there will be a little potential for price gains," he said.
ProSieben chief finance officer Lothar Lanz expected around half of the 17.5 million non-voting preference shares will be placed in Germany and the rest with international investors.
The company is also seeking a private placement 144a in the United States.
Asked about the dividend, Kofler and Lanz would not comment on market forecasts, only saying that the dividend will be "oriented towards earnings".
Analysts have forecast a dividend for 1997 of around 40 pfennigs and for 1998 of 1.50 marks.
